segments.text: ...calling is the case involving Nimbus Apollo versus U.S. Bank National Association.
So we should have Mr. Rubai for the appellant and Mr. Donovan on behalf of the appellee.
So, Mr. Rubai, you were just here.
Oh, Your Honor, I was just here someplace.
All right, how much time would you like to reserve for Rubai?
All right, whenever you're ready, Mr. Rubai, please proceed.
This is a case involving a foreclosure, and the appeal is about the fact that, and I've never actually had this happen, although I've been involved in a lot of foreclosures.
Somehow or another, the clerk issued the certificate of title.
The sale was at 26, it's two days in February.
They issued it on the 4th, and not the 10 days that's required by the statute.
And in according to how and why that happened, it turned out that one of the orders that was entered on a pre-sale objection that was filed 836 in the morning to this objection itself,
we didn't want the sale to take place at all, and we had filed an objection.
That the order that was entered on that, which was actually entered the next day, had an extra paragraph in the bottom of it, and what it said was,

the clerk is instructed to complete the necessary steps towards issuance of a certificate of title and disbursement of funds to the final judgment of foreclosure entered August 16th and pursuant to Florida law.
See, that paragraph shouldn't have been there because the clerk took that to mean, because it says,
the clerk is instructed to complete the necessary steps for a certificate of title.
If you have a foreclosure sale, unless a judge calls down with a J to cancel it, or unless there's an order entered before that date cancelling it,
they automatically just go forward with the sale, and under the statute, after 10 days, you have to file an objection within 10 days after that sale is filed.
And of course, you can have different objections based on how much was bid, who bid, how much it was, sufficiency of sale, et cetera, et cetera.
Let me ask you a threshold question here.
Your friend on the other side suggests that this issue is not preserved for review.
Preserved for review. You know what that means, right?
So can you, I assume you've read his brief.
Well, the reason it's preserved for review is because we made a motion to rehear it with the court, was denied without a hearing.
And that shouldn't have happened because we filed several, we filed an objection,
we filed a motion to rehear, we filed a motion to vacate.
We filed three motions directed to the court to have this heard.
And under the case law, I put in my brief...
What did you do to try to get it set for hearing?
Because you know that a motion for rehearing is not guaranteed.
A judge can rule on that without having a hearing.
What did you do to get a hearing set on it?
Well, you know, we call up and try to get, you have to go through draws and try to...
What do we have in our record that shows that you tried to get a hearing?
I don't think there's anything on the records.
I requested an evidentiary hearing and I filed a motion for it to be heard.
Wait, so there's a motion for that?
Yeah, I filed a motion for evidentiary hearing.
I filed, I filed, okay, so first of all, on the 20, okay, I filed a motion on 3-7-20-25,
and that's before the end of the 10 days, that would have occurred.
I filed a motion to vacate certificate of sale prematurely issued.
I also filed on the same date an objection to sale and request for an evidentiary hearing.
And then on 3-10, three days later, still before, well, I think it would have ran 3-8,
but I filed a motion for rehearing and vacate order with attached copy of order.
So I filed all three of those.
And they submitted these orders through a cover letter which attached,
it showed me being served to Gabriel Streen, who was a prior attorney way before me.
And they gave form orders just denying all of them in chambers without a hearing.
But the case law is very clear under that, there's, in my case, I got Regner and that Naker case.
Naker case, they're both very clear that the statute that,
When you make an objection like that, there has to be a hearing required.
That you get a hearing, an evidentiary hearing, a hearing.
And you can't just deny it, perfunctory like that.
I mean, so, I mean, we never got a hearing on any of it.
And the judge shortened, I mean, these clerks shortened the time improperly.
It was the fourth scheduled sale of the property, right?
It was the fourth scheduled sale.
So, in my mind now, timing of what this is occurring in this event,
we had the October hurricane that took place in 2024.
The city was all over a number of different violations that were on that.
Unfortunately, the property, by the request of the plaintiffs, had been put under receivership.
And the receiver wasn't attending any of those hearings, wasn't going to any of the,
taking care of any of these matters.
So, when my client goes down and meets with the city, you know,
they go and discuss what plans they're going to have,
with the engineer and everything else,
and get all this stuff straight with the finance and everything else.
But the city's still saying, you got a receivership order here.
Do you have any authority to do anything?
So, we made motions with the court.
The opposing counsel, not this counsel, but their underlying foreclosure counsel,
He would not agree to allow us to go ahead and go forward and do anything.
So, we're sitting there going to the city, and they're sitting there saying,
well, here's an order from Judge Williams, signed,
and this order that they made.
And the funny thing about the receivership was crazy,
because there was only one tenant in the building.
The building just needed to be repaired.
There was one tenant with the building.
All the city wanted was, you know, plans in order to, you know, get it permitted.
But it has to be, you know, you have to make the request for the permit.
It has to be the owner.
But in this case, because we have the receivership order,
we're trying to get permission from the receiver to do this stuff.
Well, the first time we brought this whole issue up to Judge Williams,
or the 30 or 45 days that it was ultimately continued for,
wasn't long enough, because when we go down there,
we can't get anything done because we, even though we're the owner,
we can't do anything because the receivership order's there.
And so we filed all kinds of emergency motions to have that receivership order
rescinded or opened or done something so we could do stuff.
The receiver wanted to sell it to a third party and make a profit off of it,
as opposed, he had not met with the city at all,
hadn't attended any of the hearings.
And my client's going down there and said,
I even put up other property to go ahead and refinance it, pay this off.
But the loan is contingent on at least having the city say,
we're dealing with these code issues that they're very concerned about.
And my client is, too, because he's trying to meet that requirement.
What the appeal is about is the fact that the statute wasn't followed at all.
And there is no case that allows you to ignore the statute.
It sounds to me like you've hitched your wagon to the part of the statute that says,
That's what you're hanging your hat on.
Just so I understand your question.
You're also concerned that the 10-day period to object was not honored.
See, this is what's unusual about this case that I've never encountered.
Now, I've heard of people filing objections, and then the clerk will dismiss it, right?
And then you go up and say that the certificate shouldn't have been issued because the objections
That's kind of out there, and they always say you reversed that, et cetera.
But I've never seen it where the clerk, because they follow, you know, they're rule oriented.
You get your sale, and you get that 10 days.
If it wasn't for that extra provision that was in there, because the certificate got
issued on 3-4, and it shouldn't have been issued at all, and it happened because an
order was submitted that added that extra language to process it, and there was no reason
for that to be in the order because the clerk processes the sale under the rules no matter
In other words, if you've got an order that says there's a sale date, right, they go for
that sale date unless they get a call from the judge or an order from the judge cancelling
So this order is entered on the 27th, which adds this extra language no matter what.
It should have just been in the dial of that objection to sale.
Because the objection to sale that's in the statute says after the sale has been made,
you have 10 days from that sale being approved by the clerk to file your objections, which
asks under Regner and the statute, Regner and NEH, I said this right in brief, Regner
It's reversed if you don't get a hearing.
They say if you don't get one—
Are those on post-sale objections versus pre-sale objections?
And this was in the statute?
Yes, it was in the statute.
